summary: Defines a padding chunk and a padding parameter for SCTP, with receiver procedures. The chunk pads a packet to any size, and the parameter pads an INIT chunk. This is useful, for example, to probe path MTU.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes you want a packet of a certain size. This lets SCTP add empty filler to a message, like putting packing paper in a box until it is the size you need.

questions: how to pad an sctp packet
what is the sctp pad chunk
how to pad an sctp init chunk
subtitle: Two empty filler containers that let SCTP senders make a packet or an INIT chunk any size they need.

tldr.problem: An SCTP sender sometimes needs a packet or an INIT chunk of a particular size, for example to probe path MTU, but has no way to add harmless filler.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4820 defines a PAD chunk (type 0x84) that enlarges a packet and a PAD parameter (type 0x8005) that enlarges an INIT chunk. Receivers simply discard both.
tldr.outcome: Senders can size packets freely in steps of 4 bytes. Misuse only wastes bandwidth, and the RFC adds no new security considerations.

today: RFC 4820 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, according to the metadata for this RFC. It builds on RFC 2960 and points to RFC 4821 for the use of the PAD chunk in path MTU discovery.

sections.title: Why Padding Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 4820 defines a padding chunk and a padding parameter for the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), together with the receiver-side procedures. The chunk pads an SCTP packet to an arbitrary size. The parameter pads an INIT chunk to an arbitrary size.

The RFC points to RFC 4821 for the use of the PAD chunk in path MTU discovery. It also warns that inappropriate use of the PAD parameter or PAD chunk can waste bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a sender wants its message to be a certain size, like testing how big a parcel the post office will carry. Padding is the empty filler that makes the parcel the right size.

sections.title: The PAD Chunk
sections.content:
A PAD chunk can enlarge a packet by 4 to 65536 bytes, in steps of 4 bytes. A packet MAY contain several PAD chunks.

The chunk has a Type of 0x84 (1 byte), Flags (1 byte), a Length (2 bytes) and then the Padding Data. Flags SHOULD be zero on transmit and MUST be ignored on receipt. Length holds the length of the Padding Data plus 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The PAD chunk is a labeled bag of nothing. The label says how big the bag is, and you can stuff in as much empty space as you need.

sections.title: What Receivers Do With a PAD Chunk
sections.content:
The Padding Data MUST be ignored by the receiver. The receiver of a PAD chunk MUST discard the chunk and continue processing the rest of the chunks in the packet.

The RFC notes that this is also the required behavior for any unknown chunk whose type has the same highest-order two bits as the PAD chunk. So a receiver that has never heard of PAD already handles it correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: When the receiver opens the bag of nothing, it throws the bag away and goes on reading the rest of the mail.

sections.title: The PAD Parameter
sections.content:
The PAD parameter pads an INIT chunk. It can enlarge the INIT chunk by 4 bytes at minimum, up to the maximum size of the INIT chunk, in steps of 4 bytes. An INIT chunk MAY contain multiple PAD parameters.

The parameter has a 2-byte Parameter Type of 0x8005, a 2-byte Parameter Length (the Padding Data length plus 4), and the Padding Data. It MAY be included only in the INIT chunk and MUST NOT be included in any other chunk.

The receiver MUST silently discard it and continue with the rest of the INIT chunk. As a result, the size of the COOKIE parameter generated in the INIT-ACK MUST NOT depend on whether a PAD parameter was present, and the receiver MUST NOT include the PAD parameter in any State Cookie parameter it generates.
sections.plainLanguage: The PAD parameter is the same kind of filler, but it only goes inside the very first hello message. The receiver ignores it and does not copy it into the reply it hands back.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned the chunk type value 132 (0x84) to the Padding Chunk (PAD) in the CHUNK TYPES table. It assigned the parameter type value 32773 (0x8005) to Padding in the INIT Chunk Parameter Types table. Both registrations reference RFC 4820.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number list now says that 0x84 means PAD chunk and 0x8005 means PAD parameter, so everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it does not add any additional security considerations to the ones given in RFC 2960. The only risk it names elsewhere is wasted bandwidth when padding is used inappropriately.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding empty filler does not open any new doors for trouble. It can only waste space if someone overdoes it.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Set to 0x84 for all PAD chunks.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Zero on transmit, ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the Padding Data plus 4.

fields.name: Parameter Length
fields.desc: Length of the Padding Data plus 4.
